name: Cyan blue
lede: Cyan blue was once a name for a cornflower dye recommended by Robert Boyle, not the printer's cyan of today.

sections.title: Boyle's cornflower blue
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium records that in the seventeenth century Boyle recommended a blue dye prepared from cornflower petals, *Centaurea cyanus* [1]. Some eighteenth-century watercolor books gave the color as cornflower blue, Boyle's blue or cyan blue [1]. The color was criticized in 1738, and there is no evidence it was ever sold commercially [1].

The name comes from the Greek for blue, kept in words like *cyano-* [2]. Today's cyan is counted among the spectral hues, the bands seen in a rainbow or through a prism [3]. See [[cyan]], [[cerulean]] and [[light-blue]]. The Compendium also files the name as a synonym of cornflower blue, so it is a pigment-literature name, not a modern screen color [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is rare in museum paint. It appears in 0.06% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (14 paintings, as photographed) [4]. It peaks in the 1800s, at 1.6 times the expected rate [4].

origin.named_after: Greek kyanos, blue (via the cornflower, Centaurea cyanus)

notes.cite: ColorHub archive, 23,781 museum paintings as photographed (data/graph/fieldnotes, CIEDE2000)

questions.q: Which flower gave the dye called cyan blue?
True or false: Boyle's cornflower dye was sold commercially.

openers: Cyan blue once meant a cornflower dye that no one ever sold.
